operations.evidence: The principal accountable person must establish and operate a complaints system that allows residents and other building users to raise relevant complaints.
A complaints system's existence does not prove that individual complaints are handled effectively.
Relevant complaints concern structural failure, spread of fire or the performance of an accountable person.
A routine service or maintenance request must not automatically be classified as a relevant complaint.
The PAP must keep a record of each relevant complaint for seven years.
A retention period does not establish that records are complete or accurate.
The record must include complaint information, AP response steps, regulator involvement and the outcome.
Recorded fields do not prove the adequacy of the investigation or outcome.
More than one relevant complaint about the same issue within seven years is treated as a recurring relevant complaint.
Similarity between complaints requires issue-level evidence and must not be inferred from keywords alone.
The complaints system should support impartial and fair treatment of issues raised.
A policy statement is not proof that treatment was impartial in a particular case.
Residents should be involved and consulted when the complaints process is established or changed.
Consultation does not transfer statutory responsibility to residents.
Residents must be told what a relevant complaint is, how to raise it, how it will be handled and expected investigation and response timings.
Published information does not prove that every resident received or understood it.
The process must describe how and when issues can be escalated to BSR and provide contact details.
An escalation route does not mean BSR will accept every issue as a relevant complaint.
People raising issues must be able to challenge responses and may appoint a representative when necessary.
Representation does not alter the evidential requirements for the complaint.
An existing complaints system may be adapted; a separate building-safety complaints process is not always required.
Adaptation must still cover the statutory building-safety complaint requirements.
The PAP must publish a complaints policy explaining relevant complaints, responsibilities and how the system works.
Publication alone does not prove operational compliance.
The latest policy must be provided to accountable persons and residents, and other APs must understand and use the process.
A distribution claim requires delivery evidence and must not be inferred from file creation.
Complaint information should be clearly displayed and accessible, with channels such as email, telephone, online and in person considered.
Availability of channels does not prove accessibility for every resident.
Complaints should be prioritised by identified risk rather than receipt order, tracked through investigation and answered with reasons, actions and timeframes.
Risk prioritisation requires case-specific assessment and must not be reduced to a generic queue score.
For this guidance, a resident is over 16 and lives in or owns a residential unit.
This definition does not determine tenancy, ownership or capacity in a specific case.
Accountable persons and the PAP are responsible for repair and maintenance of common parts and management of fire-spread and structural-failure risks.
Responsibility does not prove that a defect exists or that a duty was breached.
Residents can complain about building-safety risks or the performance of an AP or PAP.
A complaint is an allegation and not a verified safety finding.
Concerns may cover AP or PAP communications, responses to concerns and management of building-safety risks.
Poor communication and physical safety risk are distinct issues and should not be conflated.
Flammable external cladding is given as an example of a possible relevant building-safety concern.
The example does not establish the material or combustibility of a named building.
Missing or non-working fire doors or smoke extraction that may increase fire spread are examples of relevant concerns.
A concern requires building-specific inspection or evidence before attribution.
Collapse, cracks and parts falling from a building are examples of structural-safety concerns.
A visible crack alone does not establish structural failure or severity.
The PAP must display their name and contact details clearly in the building.
A displayed name does not prove that the correct legal PAP has been identified.
APs must explain relevant complaints, expected responses and all stages of the process; residents can request a copy.
Availability of a copy does not prove the process was followed in a case.
The complaints process should be available in formats such as large text, easy read, braille or audio, with language or format support requested from an AP.
Listing alternative formats does not prove they were supplied.
A resident may appoint a representative to raise concerns.
A representative's involvement does not verify the underlying complaint.
A complaint can be referred to BSR when a person cannot complain, feels unable to raise concerns or is dissatisfied with the PAP response.
Referral eligibility does not guarantee BSR investigation or enforcement.
The PAP must acknowledge receipt and say whether the issues are accepted or rejected as a relevant complaint.
Acceptance or rejection is a procedural decision and not a final safety determination.
For an accepted complaint, the PAP must investigate, provide an expected response date, explain actions taken and give a timeline for remaining issues.
An investigation timeline is not evidence that corrective work is complete.
Final responses, photos, videos, correspondence and action information can support a BSR referral; BSR decides relevance and does not disclose personal details without consent.
Submitted material may be incomplete, and privacy protection does not imply the complaint is substantiated.
Clients, principal designers, principal contractors and accountable persons in scope must keep a digital building-information record.
The duty's applicability depends on role and building classification.
